about.blurb: A reworking of all the narrative prose in The Dunwich Legacy Campaign Guide for Arkham Horror, compatible with the story as told on the scenario cards. It changes nothing mechanically about The Dunwich Legacy but quite a bit about the story’s texture.

sections.title: Translator’s Note
text: Any translation of a well-known work is an imposition on the world that it is the translator’s custom and duty to justify. The justification is even more necessary when the translator, full of hubris, would also be an emender, and take upon himself the reimagining of entire scenes in the original, with the consequence of radically changing almost everything. And yet I think the unholy work I desecrate and blaspheme in these pages profits by that desecration and blasphemy, the way a holy work benefits from worship and reverence. I leave it to you, dear reader, to decide.—Olaus Wormius

sections.title: Preface
text: What is *The Dunwich Legacy of Olaus Wormius*? It is a reworking of all the narrative prose in *The Dunwich Legacy Campaign Guide* for Arkham Horror and is compatible with the story as told on the scenario cards. It changes nothing mechanically about *The Dunwich Legacy* but quite a bit about the story’s texture. In this preface, I discuss my goals for this reworking. Then I talk briefly about how to use it in your game.

First, I aimed to change the style of the campaign’s writing. The original has several merits. It is efficient, unpretentious, and clear—all virtues that are hard to find in Lovecraft’s own writing. But it sometimes leans on genre tropes and falls short of being as immersive as the game itself. I hope my revisions help the story unfold more subtly, personally, and surprisingly, with Henry Armitage, Seth Bishop, and the rest coming across as more dynamic and alive. This does not mean you have to read more: I aimed to keep the quantity of writing about the same. There’s one exception: I’ve added a new interlude between Scenarios II and III so that players wanting to take on a side scenario can do so with a little more narrative justification. A European or Egyptian adventure would still be a stretch in this little gap, but taking on a mystery in the vicinity of Arkham is now credible.

I have also revised the plot and other story details to make the campaign’s narrative more coherent. The investigators are less naïve and, at the end of the story, less passive. The (human) antagonist’s motivation now has bones. Without giving anything away, his presence is woven into the campaign earlier than in the original *Legacy*. I occasionally incorporate investigator- and class-specific framing, too, so that the narrative responds in small ways to the Lead Investigator’s identity—Most often where these nods felt almost necessary.

My secondary goal was to strengthen the connection between *The Dunwich Legacy* and Lovecraft’s *Dunwich Horror* by addressing inconsistencies between the campaign and Lovecraft’s story and more elegantly synthesizing the parts that overlap. Less elegantly, as you can see, I’ve included footnotes.[^1] You can safely avoid these.

sections.title: How To Use This Work
text: It’s very easy. Instead of reading the narrative blocks at the beginning of scenarios and in scenario resolutions, read this instead. I direct you back to *The Dunwich Legacy Campaign Guide* when you have a choice to make, something to note in the campaign log, etc.

In other words, nothing affecting the mechanics of the card game happens in *The Dunwich Legacy of Olaus Wormius*, but everything story-related occurring outside the round structure of the card game does.

One difference between this document and the campaign guide is the inclusion of investigator-conditional narrative blocks. The way these work is probably self-evident, but if you’re confused and don’t know which one to pick, just skim them and choose the one you think fits the Lead Investigator best.

My writing presupposes the Lead Investigator as the main character (the “you”) in each scene. But what if you are not playing solo—Where are the other investigators? Depending on the situation, they could be right there with the Lead Investigator, taking a backseat during whatever is happening, or, if it makes narrative sense, somewhere else doing things they would likely be doing. If the Lead Investigator is traveling by train to a destination in rural Massachusetts, for example, the other investigators may be sitting down the aisle. If the Lead Investigator is listening to a distraught librarian, the other investigators could learn about the librarian’s plight from the Lead Investigator afterwards and then join up with them.

sections.title: Disclaimer
text: This is a labor of love and interpretation and reflects my own sensibilities. I in no way want to suggest that the original is not good enough, but to supplement it with a variation, a “take,” that, after all, owes everything to the existence of that original. My hope is that I help breathe new life into the first expansion and give players yet another reason to replay it.

sections.title: Timeline of The Dunwich Horror and The Dunwich Legacy of Olaus Wormius
text: _August, 1928_
Friday the 3rd. Wilbur Whateley is killed by a dog on the campus of Miskatonic University
12th-15th (probable). Wilbur Whateley’s books and manuscripts are delivered to Miskatonic University.
_September, 1928_
Sunday the 2nd. Armitage decodes Wilbur Whateley’s diary.
Tuesday the 4th. Warren and Rice call on Armitage and learn about some of his discoveries.
Wednesday the 5th. Armitage begins taking notes on Whateley’s papers.
Thursday the 6th. Armitage completes his work at the cost of his physical and mental health.
Friday the 7th. Armitage is delirious the first part of the day; late in the day he wakes, purposeful.
Saturday the 8th. Warren, Rice, and Armitage meet at the library to debate what to do.
Sunday the 9th. The Dunwich horror breaks loose. In Arkham, Armitage continues his research.
Wednesday the 12th. Armitage sees a report in the *Arkham Advertiser* about the invisible horror in Dunwich.
Friday the 13th. The Frye household is destroyed. Armitage, Rice, and Warren head to Dunwich.
Saturday the 14th. The Bishop household is destroyed. Silas and Seth Bishop escape. Armitage and the others banish the Dunwich horror.
Tuesday the 25th. Seth Bishop writes to Henry Armitage about his brother’s transformation.
_October, 1928_
Monday the 22nd. Seth Bishop consults the books of Wizard Whateley.
Wednesday the 31st. Seth Bishop’s corruption is complete. He becomes a servant of Yog-Sothoth.
_November, 1928_
Thursday, November 29th - Friday, November 30th. The events of *Extracurricular Activity*, *The House Always Wins*, and *The Miskatonic Museum*.
_December, 1928_
Wednesday, December 19th. The events of *Essex County Express*.
Thursday, December 20th. The events of *Blood on the Altar*.
Friday, December 21st. The events of *Undimensioned and Unseen*, *Where Doom Awaits*, and *Lost in Time and Space*.

notes: [^1] Please let me tell you about a small inconsistency I can’t address in my reworking, the presence of the Congregational Church in Dunwich. (This is off-limits to me because it’s a scenario card.) In *The Dunwich Horror*, this church is only named once, historically, as the place where Abijah Hoadley gave a fatal sermon against devil worship in 1747 (p. 372). The other time a Dunwich church is mentioned is in the first description of the town: “It is not reassuring to see, on a closer glance, that most of the houses are deserted and falling to ruin, and that *the* broken-steepled church now harbors the one slovenly mercantile establishment of the hamlet” (p. 371; emphasis mine). It’s reasonable to infer that there was one church in Dunwich, the Congregational, and that it was converted into Osborn’s. In the game, these are two distinct locations.

All exact dates for events in DH are given by Lovecraft himself. When coming up with dates for the events in The Dunwich Legacy of Olaus Wormius, I used Lovecraft’s timeline and suggestions in TDL, including flavor text on one of the first cards players see (on Miskatonic Quad: “A too-early winter has stripped the trees bare”). The introduction to The Miskatonic Museum also suggested the timeframe: “Several months ago, Armitage and his colleagues stopped a rampaging horror from tearing through Dunwich” (TDL, p. 9). Card art was a factor, too, and most location cards (with some exceptions, like Bishop’s Brook) show environments that fit the implied late fall setting. That said, several locations in Where Doom Awaits look green and downright summery (see Ascending Path and Frozen Spring). Luckily, it really does make narrative and thematic sense for summer and winter to become mixed up in this scenario, and I tried to make the most of the seeming inconsistency via Zeb’s comment on p. 22.

prologue.title: Prologue
prologue.body:
“But it’s not like Warren. Francis, maybe. But not Warren.”

You are standing with Dr. Henry Armitage across from the campus of Miskatonic University. The klaxon of a swerving automobile alerted you to the elderly librarian dashing across College Street. His papers had scattered over the sidewalk, and as you helped gather them, he tried to explain his discomposure. Two of his colleagues, Professors Warren Rice and Francis Morgan, are missing.
prologue.readOneOfTheFollowing: The Lead Investigator reads one of the following and then skips to the non-grayed text.
prologue.miskatonic: _If the Lead Investigator has the Miskatonic trait_: Armitage is a venerable and beloved fixture on campus. A trip he took with Warren and Rice in September became the subject of odd rumors among students and faculty. You never heard any credible account of what happened.
prologue.mystic:
_If the Lead Investigator is a Mystic_: You made Armitage’s acquaintance in October at a meeting for people interested in psychic phenomena. Almost no one there knew what they were talking about—Planchettes, theosophy, spectral photography—but Armitage did. He introduced himself to you at the end of the evening, and you shivered when you shook his hand. He felt it too.

“We have seen things these people haven’t,” he said. “I can tell.”
prologue.charlieKane: _If the Lead Investigator is Charlie Kane_: Dr. Armitage and his wife attended one of your fundraisers once; he gently quipped that he preferred the pretzels to your politics.
prologue.seekerOrKohaku: _If the Lead Investigator is a Seeker or Kohaku_: You know Armitage well. Your research often leads you to the university library, and he has been unfailingly helpful. Recently, he remarked, “Myths, folklore, the occult…Is it the fascination of the unknown that draws you to these subjects, or escape from a humdrum reality? Take my word for it: don’t take your reality for granted.”
prologue.otherwise:
_Otherwise_: You recently met Armitage at a local restaurant. He forgot his book when he got up. You brought it to him as he donned his hat at the door, only then catching its title, The Witch-Cults of Old New England.

“Interesting reading,” you said.

“Yes. And, though you might not believe me, relevant. Thank you,” he said. “When I leave home without my wife, I depend on the kindness of strangers to keep me in order. But must we be strangers?” he added charmingly.

You exchanged names before he left.
prologue.tail:
Now, that dignified old man is distraught. “True, they’ve only been gone a few hours,” he is saying. “But we have a weekly engagement…Let’s just say I like to keep track of them. But how reassuring to see a familiar face! Thank you for—putting me back together.”

The sky is getting dark, and lights twinkle in windows up and down College Street. You hand the agitated librarian the last of his papers.

“Why don’t you go to the police?” you ask.

“As I said, it’s only been a few hours. I don’t think the police would take me seriously.”

“They’ll show up, I’m sure,” you say, feeling the conversation has run its course. You have things you have to do, private business this chance encounter has delayed.

Armitage takes the hint. He looks not just disappointed but stricken. Then you see it: he knows something, and whatever he knows makes him certain that all is not right in the world. The New England gentleman’s habit of restraint is all that keeps him from howling in despair.

“I know this must sound absurd. But listen: if you happen to have business on campus, could you possibly look for Warren—and if you find him, let him know I’m anxious? Or if you’re heading that direction, Francis might be at the Clover Club, the speakeasy. Everyone has their vices, and he has many. But there are worse things, believe me. That,” he says, pointing, “is my house. Please come by if anything is amiss.[^2] I have urgent work to do—work I hope is unrelated to these disappearances—or I would look for them myself.”
prologue.footnote2: Armitage lives across the street from Miskatonic University: “Armitage, hastening into some clothing and rushing across the street and lawn to the college buildings…” (DH, p. 388).

interlude1.title: Interlude I: Armitage’s Fate
interlude1.proceedToArmitagesFate1: Check Campaign Log. If *the investigators were unconscious for several hours*: Read _Armitage’s Fate 1_.
interlude1.armitagesFate1:
_Armitage’s Fate 1_: When you show up to Armitage’s house, Mrs. Armitage is on the phone with the police.[^3] “Officer? Someone’s here. No, I don’t think so. I’ll call you back.”

The old woman is suspicious at first, but after you introduce yourself and describe your earlier conversation with her husband, she opens up.

“Ever since that business in Dunwich and those nights he spent with that awful diary—Nothing has been the same in this house. Nothing. I don’t know where he went. He said he needed to step out. That was hours ago. There have been sirens all night. Oh, Henry, Henry…Why did you let yourself get mixed up in all this?”

“Why did he leave? He told me he’d be here.”

“He left after I showed him this,” she says, handing you a letter. “It came today but was sent in September. Our address was poorly written—It must have been lost in the mail.” You skim the letter.

“This could be very helpful,” you say. “You mentioned a diary—Could I see that too?”

“If you think it would help. The ghastly book was in some kind of code. His notes on it are in the envelope on his desk, along with his own diary.”
interlude1.footnote3: Though Armitage seems to be a bachelor in DL, in DH he has a wife: “That evening, just as twilight fell, he finished his terrible perusal and sank back exhausted. His wife, bringing his dinner, found him in a half-comatose state…” (p. 400).
interlude1.armitagesFate2:
_Armitage’s Fate 2_: Dr. Armitage is right at the door, with his coat on, when you knock.

“You’re here! Wonderful. I feared the worst. But I just learned something dreadful. I was on my way to the museum.”

“The museum!” you remark. “At this hour?”

“Yes, yes. I’ll explain. But first, tell me what happened. Any news of Francis and Warren?”

You tell Dr. Armitage about the evening’s events. “I’ll go to the museum,” you say. “You stay here. But I need to know what’s going on.”

“Yes, you do,” says the old man. “I’ll tell you everything I know. And then I’ll show you the letter my wife handed me when I got home. Fate is against us: If I had received it sooner, I might have prevented all of this. It was sent two months ago, but the address was poorly written and only made its way here today.”

interlude1a.title: Interlude I-A: False Leads
interlude1a.body:
You had nothing to do with the banishment of the Dunwich horror. When Armitage asked you to find his friends, he drew you into a sorcerous maelstrom whose intended victims were him, Rice, and Morgan, the ones who closed the gate on Yog-Sothoth, not you. But now you have made yourself visible to that same entity. The thought is not a pleasant one. You are dwelling on it when you enter your bedroom a little after dawn.

You lie down and can’t sleep. You realize that you are trembling.

Then the phone rings.
interlude1a.proceedToPart1: Check Campaign Log. If *the investigators rescued Dr. Henry Armitage*: Proceed to _Part 1_.
interlude1a.proceedToPart2: If *Dr. Henry Armitage was kidnapped*: Skip to _Part 2_.
interlude1a.part1:
_Part 1_: It’s Armitage. You describe what happened at the museum.

“I’m glad you’re alive,” he says. “I have news, too. I finally did call the police an hour ago. The detective I spoke with had had a very busy night and didn’t want to talk, but when I pressed him, he told me a cab driver called to report suspicious activity. He saw hooded figures ushering a professional-looking man into a vehicle. Alarmed, the driver followed the car onto the Newburyport Turnpike. He lost them about ten minutes north of Boston. ‘Now, I don’t know if that was a friend of yours or not,’ the detective said, ‘But sounds like it could be from your descriptions.’”

You ask what Armitage intends to do. “I’ll go to Cambridge. Whateley visited Harvard in looking for the Necronomicon, and these new followers of Yog-Sothoth may have gone there to make sure no copy falls into our hands.[^5] The Arkham Police Department has already alerted the authorities in Boston. I might as well follow up with them while I’m there. I have to do something, by God. I fear that my very presence endangers my wife.”

“What about Dunwich? The Bishops?” you ask.

“I’ve written to Seth Bishop, care of Osborn’s General Merchandise.[^6] I intend to go there as soon as I get back.”
interlude1a.footnote5: When Armitage denies Whateley access to the Necronomicon, Whateley memorably responds, “‘Wal, all right, ef ye feel that way about it. Maybe Harvard won’t be so fussy as yew be’” (DH, p. 386). Because Armitage warns the librarians there about Whateley’s intentions, Whateley’s trip to the Widener Library is a failure.
interlude1a.footnote6: Seth Bishop’s home is destroyed in DH; in TDL, the “Bishops’ farmhouse” isn’t destroyed until Scenario V (p. 17). See footnote 11.
interlude1a.part2:
_Part 2_: It’s Mrs. Armitage.

“I have news about Henry. I thought you should know,” she says. Her voice is hoarse from crying. “A detective called. He told me a cab driver saw hooded figures ushering someone matching Henry’s description into a vehicle. The driver followed them onto the Newburyport Turnpike, southbound. He lost them about ten minutes north of Boston. The detective telephoned the Boston authorities. And he said to be hopeful: the cab driver had given them a plate number and detailed descriptions.”

“Thank you, Mrs. Armitage,” you say. “That does sound hopeful.” You talk a little more and then hang up.

You have little choice but to wait for the police investigation to conclude. True, you can trace all this mayhem to the village of Dunwich; but the water seems to have left that spring already, and it’s not clear that going there would do anyone any good. Then you recall the Bishops—But what can you do for them? That business was Armitage’s, wasn’t it? Unsatisfied, you decide to study the materials you’ve gathered.
interlude1a.sideScenario: If you have the Experience and the desire to do so, this is a good narrative opportunity to do a side scenario. Otherwise, proceed to _Scenario III: The Essex County Express_.

interlude2.title: Interlude II: The Survivors
interlude2.body:
_Check Campaign Log. If the O’Bannion gang has a bone to pick with the investigators_: As you emerge from the hidden chamber, you see one of the black-clad men from Arkham running to the cars they came in.

“Get in! Get in!” he yells to the mobster lucky enough to have stayed behind with the vehicles.

The mobster puffs his cigarette. “What gives?” he asks. “Find ’em?”

“Get in, dammit! These bumpkins are loony.”

“Where’s Billy?”

“Eaten, for Chrissake. Get in!!!”

He does. The cars zoom away.

You have found Silas Bishop and seen Seth’s handiwork, but where is Seth? And where is everyone else? Then you hear a cry. A figure comes racing across the field between Dunwich and Sentinel Hill. Just one figure—Or are there more?
interlude2.drHenryArmitageRescued: _Check Campaign Log. If Dr. Henry Armitage is not listed under “Sacrificed to Yog-Sothoth” AND “The investigators rescued Henry Armitage”_: “There you are! What a stroke of luck, running into you on College Street that night. But listen: We have work to do. I don’t know how the evil designs Wilbur spent years pursuing have been realized by this novice in the space of a month, but I do know this: Yog-Sothoth is at the threshold of our world. We must find Seth Bishop. If even a tendril of his master finds its way through that gate, the world is lost. But Seth is flesh and blood. Seth can be thwarted. We must act soon: the solstice is tomorrow.”
interlude2.drHenryArmitageKidnapped: _Check Campaign Log. If Dr. Henry Armitage is not listed under “Sacrificed to Yog-Sothoth” AND “Dr. Henry Armitage was kidnapped”_: “What—You? You came all the way here? I never thought to hope. What a stroke of luck, running into you on College Street! Now we must find our adversary. If even a tendril of his master finds its way through that gate, the world is lost. And we must act soon: the solstice is tomorrow, and I believe that is when he will try the door.”
interlude2.professorWarrenRice: _Check Campaign Log. If Professor Warren Rice is not listed under “Sacrificed to Yog-Sothoth”_: Later, Professor Rice remarks, “When my last adventure in Dunwich ended, I vowed to come back. The region’s language is a peculiar blend of East Anglian archaisms, modern colloquialisms, and a strain that’s harder for me to identify—a rhythmic, sort of guttural way of talking that must owe something to the town’s isolation. A linguistic study was in order, I thought. I now consider my vow fulfilled: here I am. And though I didn’t pursue that research after all, I make a new vow. I will never, ever come back here.”
interlude2.drFrancisMorgan: _Check Campaign Log. If Dr. Francis Morgan is not listed under “Sacrificed to Yog-Sothoth”_: A group of villagers opposed to the unwholesome rites of their neighbors soon assembles at Osborn’s. Dr. Morgan addresses them: “Armitage told me last time that my gun wouldn’t be of any use.[^11] That may be true if we face something like we did in September. But we’re up against beasts and men too. If you people have guns, pitchforks, or bayonets your great-great-grandfathers used in the Revolutionary War, it’s time to dust them off. And speaking of dust—Does anyone know if any of that powder we used last time still exists?”
interlude2.footnote11: “Morgan uncased the big-game rifle on which he relied despite his colleague’s warnings that no material weapon would be of help” (DH, p. 403).
interlude2.zebulonWhateley:
_Check Campaign Log. If Zebulon Whateley is not listed under “Sacrificed to Yog-Sothoth”_: As you walk back to his house for the evening, Zebulon explains why he did not come back last night.

“I knew something was brewing in the hills. Folks had gone missing. I heard noises afore I picked you up, not just whippoorwills but screams and worse. To tell the truth, I didn’t know if I could trust you. So Curtis stayed put, watchin’ the house until he got worried, and I took Earl out to look for the trouble. But then some of Seth’s people got us and took us up to Sentinel Hill. They tied us up and we spent the day waitin’ for death. Right before he was about to kill me, Seth just stopped that rite. I think he knew when you killed Silas. He dropped his wicked knife and put his head in his hands. That’s when we got free and ran.”
interlude2.earlSawyer:
_Check Campaign Log. If Earl Sawyer is not listed under “Sacrificed to Yog-Sothoth”_: Back at Zeb Whateley’s house, now the base of operations for everyone working against Seth, Earl remarks:

“By golly, I think the Lord must be bitter mad at folks here and I think the Devil himself has gotten into Seth. Now I know the Devil took some other name, but that’s just like him. And I sure am glad you folks from Arkham done come up, but as my Gram said, if there’s a bully, better run and pray for his soul later than fight him and get caught in Satan’s meshes. And I hope you don’t mind my saying, but I think Satan’s already caught you in his meshes and Lord I don’t know but that it’s gonna be real hard to get out—But you gotta try.”

epilogue.title: Epilogue
epilogue.intro: Read the following only if the investigators won the campaign. There is only one Epilogue.
epilogue.body:
May 2, 1990.

They parked the car and climbed the path. Spring was in the air. If Jessie were a different sort of person, she might have paused to admire the yellow-green slopes of the mountains, the contrast between the lively note they struck and the more somber tone suggested by their bare, craggy tops. She was not one to listen for unheard melodies or to acknowledge spring. She had a folder in her hands and was thinking about its contents.

“How far is it?” she asked.

“Not far,” said Bill.

They reached the top of Sentinel Hill. Bill whistled. “Not a bad view, eh?”

“The town is an eyesore.”

“Dunwich? Hardly anyone lives there anymore. It won’t be a problem for long.”

“You talked to Desmond about it?”

“Yeah. It won’t be very expensive. This wasn’t,” he said, gesturing to the altar-like rock formation.

“I’m surprised it’s not a park or something. Can’t believe there’s no environmental interest.”

“No one knows about it. It’s private property.”

“Well, let’s not tell.”

“You like it then?” Bill asked.

“Yes,” said Jessie. “Yes, I do. There will need to be a road, obviously. But it’s good, it’s good. We’re only fifteen minutes from the Aylesbury Valley Mall.”

They left well before sunset. It had been decades since anyone observed the fires that used to burn on Sentinel Hill on May-Eve, and there was no fire that night. Of mysterious tremors were there none. As early as 1978 no one remembered what people once said about the whippoorwills. Now the birds were rare enough to merit a local “Save the Eastern Whippoorwill!” campaign that garnered little interest or success. They would not call from the trees of Sentinel Hill that evening. Meanwhile, in Dunwich, Arkham, and elsewhere, the true lords and inheritors of the earth ate dinner, watched TV, and went to bed—serene, primal, and foul.

intro.title: Scenario I-A: Extracurricular Activity
intro.firstScenario: _If you have not completed Scenario 1-B_: You could not shake the conviction that Armitage had a serious reason to be concerned. Miskatonic was right there: it could do no harm to oblige the old man.
intro.completedTheHouseAlwaysWins: _If you have completed Scenario 1-B_: After the disaster at the Clover Club, you race to the university. You need to tell Armitage what happened, but before that, you need to find Rice. You fear it’s too late.

noResolution.title: No Resolution
noResolution.body:
_If no resolution was reached (each investigator was defeated or resigned)_: You run as ambulance sirens wail and confusion grips the campus. Past the stately buildings and trees, past the policemen arriving too late, past the dismembered bodies of two students. “Whip-poor-WILL! Whip-poor-WILL!” go the unseen birds in the branches of Miskatonic’s stately old trees. “Something’s wrong,” you say to yourself over and over, keeping time with their calls.

  • In your Campaign Log, record that Professor Warren Rice was kidnapped.
  • In your Campaign Log, record that the investigators failed to save the students. You are haunted by guilt. Add 1 {'{'}tablet{'}'} token to the chaos bag for the remainder of the campaign.
  • Each investigator earns experience equal to the Victory X value of each card in the victory display. Each investigator earns 1 experience as they reflect on the night’s events.
    • _Experience_: {xp}
  • If this is the first scenario of the campaign, proceed to Scenario I–B: The House Always Wins. Otherwise, proceed to Interlude I: Armitage’s Fate.

resolution1.title: Resolution 1
resolution1.body:
_Resolution 1_: “I heard Armitage come by earlier and hoped he’d come back,” Warren Rice says after you rescue him from the closet where he was confined. “When you’re tied up and gagged, there’s not much you can do but hope. I don’t know who or what they were. I remember little and saw less. But the smell—I knew the smell.”

You press him on this detail, but he divulges no more. Like Armitage, he knows something but fears disclosing it.

You lead him from the faculty offices as sirens wail and confusion grips the campus. You hear screams, and Rice gasps when he trips over a severed arm in the quad. You wonder, disturbingly, if you could have prevented that. “Whip-poor-WILL! Whip-poor-WILL!” go the unseen birds in the university’s stately trees. Before you reach the gates, Rice stops and cries out, “Good God! What about Francis? Where is he?” You usher him off campus. “The Clover Club, if we’re lucky,” you say.

  • In your Campaign Log, record that *the investigators rescued Professor Warren Rice*. Any one investigator may choose to add Professor Warren Rice to their deck. This card does not count toward that investigator’s deck size.
  • In your Campaign Log, record that *the investigators failed to save the students*. You are haunted by guilt. Add 1 {'{'}tablet{'}'} token to the chaos bag for the remainder of the campaign.
  • Each investigator earns experience equal to the Victory X value of each card in the victory display.
    • _Experience_: {xp}
  • Proceed to Scenario I–B: The House Always Wins.

resolution2NotMiskatonic.title: Resolution 2
resolution2NotMiskatonic.body:
_If you received Resolution 2 and the Lead Investigator does NOT have the Miskatonic trait_: “That’s right, there’s a fire. Out, now,” you command a bleary-eyed student. Some of the dorm’s residents don’t take the alarm seriously, and a shrewd young man demands to know who you are and why they should listen to you. But with desperate coaxing you lead everyone out the back door. You hear a tremendous crash from inside, a shriek—And then nothing. When you investigate, there’s no sign of the creature.

The police arrive and you slink off, hurrying to the faculty offices in search of Rice. But if he was ever there, he’s gone now.

intro.title: Scenario I-B: The House Always Wins
intro.body: La Bella Luna looks like a sleepy, shabby Italian restaurant. But people in the know stride in, nod at the waiter, pass through a kitchen where an old woman is always puttering, and open a broom closet doubling as the front door of the opulent Clover Club. You are one of those people and, according to Armitage, so is Francis Morgan.

intro.jimOrMarie:
_If the Lead Investigator is Jim or Marie_: “Didn’t know you’d be on tonight,” says the bouncer at the vestibule. “In fact, didn’t think you’d play here ever again.”

“Not here for music,” you say. “Business.”

“Business? Well golly, I thought music was your business,” he says. “Take care. I’m watching you.”
intro.criminal:
_If the Lead Investigator has the Criminal trait_: “Hold it. You know you’re not welcome here,” says the bouncer at the vestibule.

“I had no idea,” you say.

“Don’t play smart with me. Scram,” he says.

“I go where I please, Otto. Do I need to remind you how we met?”

Otto grimaces and reluctantly stands aside. “I’m watching you,” he says.

“Of course you are. I’m the most interesting thing here,” you say, sounding more confident than you really are.
intro.daniela:
_If the Lead Investigator is Daniela, Nathaniel, Roland, or Tommy_: “You sure you’re in the right place?” asks the bouncer at the vestibule.

“Yes,” you say. “Quite sure.”

“The people here—They’re just having a good time. Don’t cause any trouble.”

“I won’t if you won’t,” you say.

“Yeah all right. Go on in. But we’re watching you.”

As if on cue, the ground rumbles and the Clover Club collapses like a house of cards. Only feet away from the establishment, you both watch, astonished.

“‘Happy,’ I said! Die happy! That’s the most important part. The dying’s not so necessary. Not yet anyway. Let’s go, friend. Armitage put you up to this, didn’t he?”

_Resolution 3_: “Peter Clover, owner,” says the man you rescued, shaking your hand. You stand on a deserted corner a block away from the Clover Club.

“A pleasure, Mr. Clover. I was looking for a friend of mine before things got so rowdy.”

“Sorry to disappoint. I’m clearly not your friend – But I am grateful.”

Two Chryslers pull up. Doors slam. Cartridges click. “Peter! Thank God you’re all right. Otto’s dead. What happened?” says the striking woman who steps from the first car.

intro.title: Scenario II: The Miskatonic Museum
intro.body:
You have learned the story of the Dunwich horror.

In 1913, a woman in the forlorn town of Dunwich gave birth to twins. One was an invisible monster that would some day be big enough to crush a barn. The other, more human twin was a boy named Wilbur. Wilbur Whateley was brought up in a house devoted to sorcery and madness. He matured fast, hiding his corrupt body from the few people with whom he spoke, protecting his twin, bringing it cattle to devour. By 1927, the two were on their own. The grandfather who had taught Wilbur the Whateleys’ eldritch lore was dead, and on Halloween, 1926, Wilbur had sacrificed his own mother on Sentinel Hill, the site of the family’s horrific rites.

Whateley came to Arkham to consult the library’s translation of the Necronomicon. Armitage, suspicious, refused to let him do so. In August, Whateley returned to steal the book but was killed in the attempt. The librarian soon learned something of his history and purpose: Whateley sought to open the gate “where the Old Ones broke through of old.”[^4] Armitage, Morgan, and Rice traveled to Dunwich just in time to banish Wilbur’s rampaging twin using the Necronomicon. After this adventure, Armitage lent the book to the Miskatonic Museum, committing Harold Walsted, the museum’s curator, to keep it under lock and key in the Restricted Hall.

part2.title: Scenario II: The Miskatonic Museum
part2.body: _Part 2_: “And that, my friend, was that,” says Dr. Armitage. “Until today. Read this.”

intro.part3:
_Part 3_:

“Sep 25 1928

“Dear Mr. Armitage,

“I am sorry ahead of it for my writing. Though lettered enough I never went to school. I say thank you again for your coming to Dunwich when we needed you. But I write here to tell you it may not be all done. My brother Silas has taken ill and I fear his sickness is something wicked. For he did tell me that when that thing was abroad in the hills a voice came to him and said it was also that thing Wilbur Whateley his own twin what that he kept locked up and that it needed to come into Silas. It said it could give him gold and show him good things he knew not what. This I did learn from him when I pressed him about his leg which had grown a thick black fur like a goat and become bloated and massy. And I saw sick-green gold shining under his bed, riches from where I know not. And now you must come to Dunwich with your spells and learning for his sake. And some folks in Dunwich come by and hear Silas talk at midnight and he says the name Yog-Sothoth to them and they repeat it. Yog-Sothoth, Yog-Sothoth. It is the key [Illegible] He wants to go to Sentinel Hill. He says a door is a jar. I fear he will go there and for this shall I not lock him up and be his keeper? Please come soon with that one book.

“Signed,

“Seth Bishop”

You put the letter down. September! You wonder how these last two months have treated Seth and Silas Bishop. One thing is clear: You need to look for the Necronomicon.

But how much harder will it be to face down these strange forces if they seize the Necronomicon? Will it even be possible? As you limp down the steps of the museum, you try to correlate the contents of your racing thoughts.

resolution1BelieverOrWarden.title: Resolution 1
resolution1BelieverOrWarden.body:
_If you received Resolution 1 AND the Lead Investigator has the Believer or Warden traits_: The decision to burn the Necronomicon is not a difficult one. You tear pages from the unholy book, averting your eyes from the foul things to be seen there, and use a match to ignite them in a trash bin. Then you place the rest of the book in the fire and watch with satisfaction as it burns. Satisfaction turns to horror when the book scabs over like human flesh and begins oozing pus. “Savior or betrayer?” says a mouth that opens on the cover, “Your desire for ignorance has condemned you.” After the unwholesome grimoire is no more, you leave the museum, brooding on those words.

On the other, Wilbur Whateley needed the book to open the gate for Yog-Sothoth. You conclude that the risk of cosmic destruction outweighs any potential benefits and commit the book to a fire you start within a trash bin. As the book burns, you watch with horror as it scabs over like human flesh and begins oozing pus. “Reason?” says a mouth that opens on the cover. “No. Madness.” After the book is no more, you leave the museum, brooding on those words.

intro.title: Scenario III: The Essex County Express

intro.part1:
_Part 1_: Two weeks later, Armitage returned from Boston disappointed and frustrated. It was not that the trail had gone cold: there had never been a trail. The cab driver confessed that he’d been paid to make a false report. There had been no vehicle, no hooded figures, no kidnapping. The police were investigating the party who paid him but wouldn’t tell Armitage anything. Meanwhile, Armitage’s letter to Seth Bishop had been sent back from Dunwich with “Return To Sender” on the unopened envelope. The words were in a hand identical to that of Seth Bishop in his earlier letter.

“I don’t know what to make of this. Mr. Bishop earnestly requested my help in September, and now he refuses even to open my admittedly belated response. I fear the worst—The corruption has spread, and it affects him.”

“What do we do?” you ask.

“We go to Dunwich. I can arrange things with one of the villagers I met in September. The winter solstice is coming. I believe Wilbur would have unlocked the “gate” on Sentinel Hill on the equinox or Halloween if he hadn’t been killed. If there is further evil brewing in Dunwich, I expect it will happen on the solstice.[^7] We don’t have much time.”
intro.footnote7: Throughout the Dunwich Horror, monumental events in Wilbur’s life and rituals on Sentinel Hill often coincide with important holidays in the pagan calendar. He is born on Candlemas (Imbolc) between the winter and spring solstices (p. 374). May Eve and Halloween are especially important (p. 380). May-Eve is when Wilbur is conceived (p. 387); his mother is killed on Halloween, when “fire burned on Sentinel Hill as usual” (p. 383). His grandfather dies on Lammas (pp. 381-382). Lovecraft constantly draws attention to the significance of these holidays and when introducing the story’s climax writes, “The Dunwich horror itself came between Lammas and the equinox in 1928” (p. 387).
intro.part2:
_Part 2_: You spoke to Mrs. Armitage daily in the two weeks following her husband’s disappearance. You both grew less and less hopeful. Then came the awful news: The cab driver confessed that he’d been paid to make a false report. There had been no vehicle, no hooded figures, no kidnapping. The police were investigating the party who paid him but could not disclose what they had learned. Meanwhile, the letter her husband sent to Seth Bishop came back marked “Return To Sender.”

“Very discouraging,” you sigh over the line.

“It is,” she agreed. “And strange. I saw Mr. Bishop’s earlier letter. He wrote in a sort of crabbed, crude way. ‘Return To Sender’ was written by the same man, I’m certain.”

You have no leads in Arkham. You must go to Dunwich. The name of a villager who might be helpful recurs in Armitage’s account. Eventually, you’re able to phone him. The next day, you head to the railroad station.
intro.part3:
_Part 3_: The train to Aylesbury Station, where one Zebulon Whateley (a distant relative of Wilbur himself) is to pick you up, soon leaves the lowlands of Arkham behind.

It carries you into the shadows of the Wapack Mountains, through forests that resent the intrusion of noisy modern life into their domain, close to the edges of sheer ravines. The open spaces you pass—fields with ragged livestock, meadows with twisted old sycamores—look cheerless, lifeless. It’s December, but there’s no snow on the ground. The world is naked and drear. Despite this, there is comfort in the loneliness. You remember how, right after that terrible night in Arkham, you feared you had attracted the attention of the inscrutable Yog-Sothoth. But in this quiet, gray country, in this noisy train car, you have never felt more unnoticed and unnoticeable.

Then the train stops.

resolutions.defeat:
_Investigator Defeat_: In the word there was an end, the final syllable OTH. YOG, though, is an angle upon which, not below which, is the fulcrum YOU. When there was time, space will be its illusion. Now, here, it and it are never, like YOU, just potential, not the angle. Like you, a thousand helpless geometries that be not... “The hyphen!” cries an old man. “The hyphen! Escape through the hyphen.” You fly toward the hyphen, the pause, the slit in the gate, screaming.

You come to in cold woods at the bottom of a steep ravine. You are still screaming, but the terror gives way to dumb shock. Your hands are clammy and slow-moving as you fight leafless branches to the top. You are barely aware of what looks like a long-deserted train car whose front hangs over the slope. Then you see your luggage inside through a huge tear in the steel. There are no bodies. “It happened a long time ago,” you remind yourself. No: It just happened. You’re here, in the world you live in. You walk.

resolution1.title: Resolution 1
resolution1.body:
_Resolution 1_: If “Yog-Sothoth is the key,”[^8] you say to yourself, quoting something you remember from Armitage’s account, “I’m going to have to change that lock.” You watch as the gate closes, sucking the presences it sent forth back into itself. The Essex County Express chugs across the bridge as if nothing had happened. Even the rear train cars are back where they were, perfectly intact.

“What was that bang?!” a young woman yells out.

“Not sure,” you say, a statement both true and untrue. You make your way back to your seat.

The passengers in your car are murmuring, confused but oblivious to the gravity of what just happened. You notice the car isn’t as full as it was when you left. Not everyone made it out, you realize. The woman across from you places her handbag in the seat where her husband had been.

intro.title: Part IV: Blood on the Altar
intro.body:
There’s silence for the first twenty minutes of your drive from Aylesbury to Dunwich. Then your driver, Zebulon Whateley, breaks it.

“You heard, I guess, what those Arkham men did back September. I saw some of what there was to see. Thought when Wizard Whateley died that my family’s bad part might die with him. Wrong. Thought the same when Lavinny went. Wrong there too. And when I heard about Wilbur, I thought all the wrong that could ever be was gone, seein’ as it was all bound up in him. Wrong yet again.”

“How are things in Dunwich now?” you ask.

“Worse than wrong.”

“I heard Silas Bishop was sick,” you venture.

“I know the Bishops way back. Old family, old as us Whateleys. Seth and Silas weren’t bad folks. Right before that thing up and took down their house, they ran out the back door and hid at the brook and then went on to the Coreys’ place. Missed our hunting party with the Arkham men by ten minutes, I heard.[^10] Well, Mrs. Corey put them up, and that’s right about when Silas got sick.”

“How is he now?”

“There’s folks who seen him and folks who haven’t. Folks who seen him are mad as March hares.”

“And Seth?”

“Seth’s the maddest of them all.”

You pull up to a dilapidated house on the edge of town. It’s darker than it ever gets in Arkham. The wind is frigid.

“Almost Yule and no snow on the ground,” says Zeb. “Not good.”

Two men come out of the house. One has a pudgy, friendly face and introduces himself as Earl Sawyer. The other is holding a kerosene lantern and says he’s Zeb’s cousin Curtis.

“They gonna be all right?” Earl asks Zeb.

“Yes, Earl. Don’t run off—I need your help stacking this firewood.”

“Tonight?!” asks Earl, looking over the firewood in the back of Zeb’s truck.

“Yes, Earl. Tonight.”

Curtis shows you to a little cot in a windowless room while Zeb and Earl talk outside.

When you wake up the next morning, no one is there. The firewood is still in the back of the truck. Full of misgivings, you cross a field into the village of Dunwich. It’s already late in the day.
intro.footnote10: In The Dunwich Horror, the Bishop housekeeper, Sally, is on the telephone with Zeb when the Bishop household is destroyed. (Seth Bishop is with her inside.) The call concludes when she reports, “O help, the haouse is a’cavin’ in’” (p. 406). When Armitage and his entourage come to the ruin, “nothing dead or living was found in either of the collapsed shells which had been the Bishop house and barn” (p. 407). The Coreys’ house is mentioned as the meeting-place of the villagers who decide to accompany Armitage to Sentinel Hill (p. 406), so it seems a likely destination for the fleeing brothers.

The odor is an atrocity. A single long feeler with a rudimentary, toothy orifice at its end searches along the chamber floor for something before it, too, flattens and shrivels. Then spherical, iridescent organs break through the thing’s belly and fly from the room.

_♦ Resolution 2_: You have studied the Necronomicon extensively but cautiously since acquiring it. Though most of the text instructs the reader in the most depraved and profane mysteries, spells appended by a later author include works of banishment and purification. “‘Contra spiritualem carnis corruptionem,’” you whisper to yourself, holding the book before you as Silas Bishop strains his chains. “I think this is the one.”

resolution2.part2a: _♦ Resolution 2a_: Possession of the Necronomicon confers immense power on the possessor, no matter how much they know about magic. You know many arcane secrets, but it holds your lore in utter contempt. It asks that you let its alien intelligence take over, that you suppress your own power and make yourself its vessel. You do.
resolution2.part2b: _♦ Resolution 2b_: The book agrees. Then it takes over. It exults in displays of power. Its alien intelligence hijacks yours, and you begin to speak.
resolution2.part2c: _♦ Resolution 2c_: “Matter to matter, spirit to spirit,” you chant in seven tongues. Reality hears you. It bristles at the trespass of Yog-Sothoth. It attacks the interloping substances responsible for this aberration, burning them up. Silas writhes, his membranous flesh shriveling and sloughing off like molted skin as he cries in agony and, eventually, relief. When the book is closed and all you hear is the whippoorwills’ disappointed silence, you lean over and take a gleaming silver pendant from the hands of the corpse—the incorrupt, fully human corpse—of Silas Bishop.

resolution3.title: Resolution 3
resolution3.body:
_♦ Resolution 3_: Frantic, resolute, you search the chamber for something that will subdue or—better yet, destroy—this creature. You reason that no one would chain up a thing like this and risk its escape without preparing a means to fight it. You finally find a sheaf of notes in Seth Bishop’s crude hand and a bottle of what looks like powder.

“This be some of that powder wherewith the Arkham men did shew the first broodling. Silas likes it not and on giving him but a grain when I fed him Mrs. Corey it made him so sick that I thought he might die. The powder shews the broodling, this we know. And so when the brood is shewn to Silas his own body sees the brood and tries to kill it with retching and sickness. That is what I think.”

You uncork the bottle and sprinkle some powder onto loose papers. If it doesn’t respond to this amount you can use more, but you have a hunch the powder might be useful later. You crumple up the poisoned papers and throw the ball into the creature’s maw.

It begins to shriek, to squeal. You watch as the powder attacks its system—here and there and then all over. When the poison afflicts a new patch of sacs and fleshy tubes, the area boils and hisses and then drops off like ash from a log, and its feelers twist and curl like kindling. In seconds, he—it—is gone.

intro.title: Scenario V: Undimensioned and Unseen
intro.body:
You and the survivors take stock of the situation at Zeb Whateley’s house. It’s night, and the whippoorwills are silent for now. But the land is watchful, and unsettling rumblings have intermittently interrupted your discussions. “And so,” says Curtis Whateley, “around Halloween—Always a bad time of year here—Seth Bishop took over. He used to keep people away from Silas and his evil talk. But at Halloween, Seth’s talk turned evil too. So people went and heard him instead—By then, Silas had changed so much he couldn’t really talk no more.”

“You said Seth wanted to help Silas. He wrote to Dr. Armitage to get help too. What changed?” you ask.

“I—I think I know. He went to Wizard Whateley’s old books, him that raised Wilbur and taught him his sorcery. That did it. Whatever he found there changed him.”
intro.drHenryArmitage:
_♦ Check Campaign Log. If Dr. Henry Armitage is not listed under “Sacrificed to Yog-Sothoth”_: “I thought all books from the Whateley estate were sent to Miskatonic,” says Armitage.[^12] Curtis looks uncomfortable. “Not all of ’em. Shoulda been, maybe. But family’s family, and some of those books go back to afore Salem.”

“So that’s how you know Seth consulted them. You took some of them from the Whateley house, and you let Seth read them,” says Armitage.

Curtis stares at the floor. “Had ’em, yes. Not all of ’em. But the worst, I think. But I didn’t know what evil would come of it.”

“No one could,” says Armitage.
intro.tail:
Another tremor shakes the house. Then the door swings open and a young woman rushes in. “The trees are a’bending up the hill! It’s just like it was! Oh my God, it’s back!”

“Gerty! What do you mean? Not like afore?” demands Curtis.

“No! Not like afore! There’s more than one!”

Already scared, the villagers panic.
intro.footnote12: “After a week of debate [Wilbur’s diary] was sent to Miskatonic University, together with the deceased’s collection of strange books” (DH, p. 392).
intro.part1Survivor:
_♦ Part 1 AND the Lead Investigator is a Survivor_: “Listen up, people!” you cry. The confusion dies down.

“I know what you’re going through. None of you asked for this evil. None of you deserve this evil. I’m just like you. I don’t want it either. But we can’t be scared right now. Panic is a luxury for people whose lives are easy. We need to calm down. We need to listen to Gerty and learn what happened.”
intro.part1NotSurvivor:
_♦ Part 1 AND the Lead Investigator is not a Survivor_: “Quiet, quiet!” you shout. Eventually your words break through the ruckus, and the people listen.

“Gerty, tell us what happened.”
intro.part1a:
_♦ Part 1A_: Gerty says she went outside when her dog started barking. She saw the woods between her home and Cold Spring Glen flatten like a pancake. At the same time, she heard a mushing sound from the opposite direction, in Ten-Acre Meadow. She saw the earth sink beneath the weight of a giant, invisible thing, a footstep of the Devil himself.

“Finally come back to the Hop-Yard, I guess,” says Curtis. “Well,” he says to you. “At least the trail is clear.”
intro.part1b: _♦ Part 1B_: Armitage, Rice, and Warren had used a sprayer full of the Powder of Ibn-Ghazi to make the original Dunwich horror temporarily visible. Fortunately, a portion of that original powder is intact; Joe Osborn runs to fetch a crop sprayer from his store. With the assistance of one of the veterans of the first Dunwich adventure, you recreate the device.
intro.part2GuardianOrWarden: _♦ Part 2 AND the Lead Investigator is a Guardian or has the Warden trait_: “You all know what’s coming,” you shout. “And you’re right. The time has come to evacuate Dunwich. But don’t just run off in a panic. You need a leader. Mr. Wheeler,” you say to Henry Wheeler, one of the townsfolk who went on Armitage’s first expedition, “I nominate you. You have a clear head and have experience with these monsters. Take these folks to Osborn’s for supplies and then make for Aylesbury using the fastest route you know. We’ll take it from here.”
intro.part2NotGuardianOrWarden:
_♦ Part 2 AND the Lead Investigator is not a Guardian or does not have the Warden trait_: “Gather what you need and evacuate, now!” you command the crowd. “Avoid Sentinel Hill. Make for Aylesbury. I’ll take it from here.”

“They have the right of it!” shouts Henry Wheeler, one of the villagers who joined Armitage’s first expedition. “Let’s be orderly and get goin’.”
intro.part2a: _♦ Part 2A_: Armitage, Rice, and Warren had used a sprayer full of the Powder of Ibn-Ghazi to reveal the original Dunwich horror. Fortunately, a portion of that original powder is intact; meanwhile, before the townsfolk ransack Osborn’s for necessities, you head there and find a crop sprayer. With the assistance of one of the veterans of the first Dunwich adventure, you recreate the device.

intro.title: Scenario VI: Where Doom Awaits
intro.drHenryArmitage:
_♦ Check Campaign Log. If Dr. Henry Armitage is not listed under “Sacrificed to Yog-Sothoth”_: Armitage stares at Sentinel Hill too and slumps, defeated. “Hubris. Hubris, folly, and shortsightedness. The door was already ajar—How else would they have come through? I should have known. I blame myself.”

“We are all to blame,” you say.

“We have to redeem ourselves,” he says. “And there’s only one way to do that.”

Curtis Whateley’s car races to Sentinel Hill. It’s dark, but the flashes from the mountaintop bask the tortured landscape in constant, ghastly scarlet.
intro.zebulonWhateley:
_♦ Check Campaign Log. If Zebulon Whateley is not listed under “Sacrificed to Yog-Sothoth”_: “Not been lights like this since Wilbur was born. Never been lights like this at midwinter.” Zeb whistles. “Would you look at that?! All green.”

You don’t understand what he means at first, but then, as the trees zoom by, you do: it may be the first day of winter, but the twisted trees encircling Sentinel Hill have sprouted leathery green leaves.

"After winter, summer,” he whispers.[^13]
intro.footnote13: “After summer is winter, and after winter summer. They wait patient and potent, for here shall They reign again” (DH, p. 385).
intro.body:
Bishop manipulated you. While you chased the invisible broods around the countryside, he was preparing his rite to open Yog-Sothoth’s gate. The extradimensional behemoths represented a threat many times greater than that of their predecessor, but they were just distractions. The door was ajar; now it’s creaking open.

You step out of the car at the base of Sentinel Hill.

part1.body:
_♦ Part 1_: There’s a black Chrysler parked here. Its door is hanging open. It gleams ominously in the weird red light. As you approach, you see a man in a fedora slumped over the steering wheel, presumably dead.

A well-dressed woman steps from the woods, flanked by two mobsters. She’s pointing a gun at you. You recognize her as Naomi O’Bannion.

“Who is he to you?” she says, motioning with her gun to the dead man.

“I’ve never seen him in my life,” you say.

“Wait. You again?!” she says. “Of all the godforsaken places… What are you doing here?”

“Hunting down a man named Seth Bishop.”

“Me too. He’s the one who turned Vinny against me,” she says, gesturing again to the body. “All it took was a sack of ancient coins that can’t possibly be clean and a set of strange new religious beliefs.”

“Tell me more,” you say.

“As far as I understand it: Bishop pays Vinny; Vinny goes to a cabbie and has him bring a tall tale to the police; when the police discover the cabbie’s story doesn’t add up, the cabbie points his finger at Vinny. And that’s when Vinny points his finger at me! The police questioned me last night and I chased him all the way here this morning. Oh yes. I also learned it was Doomsday,” she concludes, pointing to the red mountaintop.

“You should leave,” you say. “Bishop’s dangerous.”

“Well, so am I,” she says.

resolution1.body: _♦ Resolution 1_: Seth looked into this book hoping to find a cure for his brother. Generations of Whateleys combed it for secrets, condemning themselves to madness and decay. The doom of two families—perhaps the doom of the world. You read:
resolution1.verse:
I AM THE PORTER OF THE OLD ONES.
I SHOW THE WAY TO UNKNOWABLE YOG.
AT THE BEHEST OF DHO IS MY SERVICE,
AT THE COMMAND OF -HNA IS MY BOND.
THE GATE IS YOG-SOTHOTH
BUT I AM THE HAND THAT PUSHETH.
TAKE THESE ROBES AND DRESS YOURSELF.
TO THE NEXUS YOU MUST GO,
TO THE CONVERGENCE OF THE AEONS,
TO THE HYPHEN AT THE VOIDS,
TO OPEN, TO WATCH,
TO CLOSE.
resolution1.part1a: _♦ Resolution 1A_: The way to close the gate lies through it. Gravity flows that way now, tugging at the robes you find yourself wearing. Where did they come from? The strange clothes sit like a crystal’s sheen on your body, and your flesh looks crystal-like itself wherever they touch. You can see the blood in your veins. You feel like a glass ready to shatter. Never more fragile, you fall into the gate.

***

In the word there was an end, the final syllable OTH. When there was time, space will be its illusion. Now, here, it and it are never. Lessness returns to Formlessness, O to Void. Yog-Sothoth hovers over the Deeps.

intro.title: Scenario VII: Lost in Time and Space
intro.body:
In the annals of Kadath it is written: “And then you came to a place outside experience.” But Kadath has left no records and does not know you, as you will never know Kadath; how, then, was it written?[^14] How are you here?

When John Dee transcribed the formulae of the angels, he wrote, “You are so far from home that home has become a threadbare dream you can barely recall.”[^15] Of what thread, bare and twisted, was that dream made? You have followed it to the the spool.

You see Dr. Armitage leaning out the window of his house in Southside. (Southside?) It’s raining but very hot, the way it sometimes gets even in Arkham, Massachusetts, these days. You’re surprised to see him. He retired in 1930. He hated it when they modernized the library. He says:

YOU HAVE DONNED THE ROBES OF THE SORCERERS.
WHAT YOU SEE IS PAINT ON THE VOID.
THERE ARE NO ARCHES OR PATHWAYS.
YOU CANNOT WALK HERE OR SEE THESE THINGS.
THEY ARE LIES, BUT DO NOT GO WITHOUT THEM.
ALAS, NO SORCERY LASTS FOREVER!
DO NOT FIGHT HIM! DO NOT LET THE ROBES FALL FROM YOUR SHOULDERS.
intro.footnote14: “Kadath in the cold waste hath known Them, and what man knows Kadath?” (DH, p. 385)

resolutions.defeated:
_♦ Before resolving any other resolution, if at least 1 investigator was defeated_: The defeated investigators read Investigator Defeat first.

_♦ Investigator Defeat_: Your robes are in tatters and cling to you like horror. You had walked off a precipice. When you came to, you saw thousands of priestesses beckoning as one. Prismatic light pulsed in their veins. Now they sigh and beckon in doubled mirrors as you approach the one true priestess in their midst… But where you kneel to be blessed is not a place, but Yog-Sothoth. And the time you take to kneel is Yog-Sothoth, too. And the being to whom you kneel has no blessing for you, for it is Yog-Sothoth, foul, serene, and total.

resolution1.title: Resolution 1
resolution1.body:
_♦ Resolution 1_: Winter has come to Sentinel Hill. Prone, eyes wide, you watched as the starry sky brightened into dimness and then pale gray, when the snow started to fall. Now you laugh, uncertain why. All you know is that you are on Sentinel Hill, it is snowing, and it is good.

“Oh my God! Oh my God!” cries a woman’s voice you can’t quite place, though you know you heard it recently.

“What is it Gerty?” asks another voice. It sounds like an older woman.

“It’s them! At least one of ’em, anyway. Don’t know where Curtis got to. Eyes are open, looks alive—but kinda shocked, I’d say. You there, you alive?”

You silently mouth the words: “Yes. Yes.”

  • In your Campaign Log, record that *the investigators closed the tear in reality*.
  • Each investigator suffers 2 physical trauma and 2 mental trauma, as they never fully recover from their time spent outside the realm of reality.

resolution2.title: Resolution 2
resolution2.body:
_♦ Resolution 2_: Gerty had watched the mountaintop all night. Not long after Curtis drove there the red light went away. She wanted to look for him then, but the other townsfolk dissuaded her.

“You can’t go to Sentinel Hill in the thick of night, Gerty. You know that,” warned Jed.

“The light’s gone.”

“More reason not to go. Stub your toe afore you get killed.”

Gerty woke up before sunrise and raced to the window to look at the mountain. It looked like it always did, but the landscape had changed.

“Jed! Nelly! It’s snowing!”

“I thought we’d lucked out this winter,” Jed said. But he too was looking out the window in wonder.

“Let’s go. Curtis hasn’t come back,” said Gerty, serious all of a sudden.

A small search party left for Sentinel Hill. Snow on the path, already several inches deep, slowed them down, but they made it to the pillared slabs soon enough.

Jed whistled. “An ugly sight. Can’t say he didn’t deserve it, though.”

They found Seth Bishop and some of his followers, all corpses. The mutations that had afflicted them were gone, though.

“No sign of the others,” said Nelly.

“What do we do?” asked Jed.

“We have to keep looking.”

“You might not find anything. Think the Devil might have scooped them up,” said Nelly.

“We have to keep looking. We have to.”

  • The investigators win the campaign…and are never seen or heard from again.

resolution3.title: Resolution 3
resolution3.body:
_♦ Resolution 3_: Yog-Sothoth is gone. You can’t see anything. Gripped by the battle rage of a titan, you scream into the void, daring your cosmic nemesis to come back. There is no response. The emptiness terrifies you. You knew the shimmering vistas and strange pathways were illusions, the craftwork of human sorcerers who sojourned in forbidden places. You even guessed your daring battle with Yog-Sothoth was a performance, a bout, to please some wicked sentience—But what could you do? You loved the role. Moments ago you were a demigod, Heimdall on a rainbow bridge. Translucent robes fluttered around you. Now your robes are in tatters. Now you are whoever you once were, an earth being in a place outside earth and being.

A gust from who-knows-where begins blowing. The sorcery protecting you flickers. You had been a beacon, a fire, a sun; now you are an ember. The wind blows more fiercely.

You remember! You remember your name!

The ember glows red. Then it goes black.

  • In your Campaign Log, record that *Yog-Sothoth has fled to another dimension*.
  • Each investigator is _killed_.
  • The investigators win the campaign…and are never seen or heard from again.
